# CWM Interpretability: Outcome Probing on SWEbench Trajectories

**Date:** 2026-04-12  
**Branch:** `andre/feat/interp`  
**Author:** André Silva

---

## Overview

We trained linear probes on internal activations of the CWM 32B model to ask: *does the model's hidden state carry information about whether it will ultimately solve a SWEbench instance?* We ran the model on all 500 SWEbench-Verified instances, captured activations at layer 32 (mid-network), and trained logistic regression probes across three analysis axes.

---

## Setup

### Model
- **Architecture:** CWM 32B, 64 layers, hidden dim 6144, GQA + window attention (3:1 local:global ratio)
- **Inference:** TP=2, DP=4 across 8×A100-80GB (Berzelius cluster)

### Activation Capture
- Hook point: post-FFN residual at each layer (`h` after `h.add_(h_out)` in `cwm/fastgen/forward.py:786`)
- Only prefill passes are captured (CUDA graphs bypass decode-step hooks)
- Layer captured: **layer 32** (middle of the 64-layer stack)
- Due to tensor parallelism, only even TP ranks (0, 2, 4, 6) write non-zero activations — this halves the effective file yield (~50% of files contain real data)

### Dataset
- **500 SWEbench-Verified instances** extracted over 3 SLURM jobs (8h wall-clock each, with resume)
- **250 good files** (non-zero activations) after filtering TP-odd-rank empty files
- **132 pass / 118 fail** (52.8% / 47.2%) — near-balanced binary label
- Per-file subsampling to 5,000 activation rows to avoid OOM; bins capped at 50,000 rows
- Probe: L2-regularised logistic regression (PyTorch Adam, 1000 iterations, C=1.0)

### Analysis Axes
Three axes slice the same stored activations differently — no re-running the model:

1. **Token position** — where in the full context window does the token appear? (10 equal-width bins over normalised position 0→1)
2. **Tool-call index** — which tool call within the episode did this token come from? (10 equal-count bins)
3. **Stage** — what type of operation was the agent performing? (exploration / editing / testing / other-bash / submission)

---

## Results

### Axis 1: Token Position

| Bin | Normalised position | n      | Majority baseline | Val accuracy |
|-----|---------------------|--------|-------------------|--------------|
| 0   | 0.0–0.1             | 50,000 | 52.7%             | **56.7%**    |
| 1   | 0.1–0.2             | 50,000 | 52.2%             | 57.3%        |
| 2   | 0.2–0.3             | 50,000 | 51.6%             | 57.4%        |
| 3   | 0.3–0.4             | 50,000 | 51.3%             | 58.4%        |
| 4   | 0.4–0.5             | 50,000 | 50.6%             | 57.9%        |
| 5   | 0.5–0.6             | 50,000 | 51.9%             | 57.5%        |
| 6   | 0.6–0.7             | 50,000 | 52.8%             | 58.9%        |
| 7   | 0.7–0.8             | 50,000 | 53.8%             | **58.9%**    |
| 8   | 0.8–0.9             | 50,000 | 57.0%             | 58.6%        |
| 9   | 0.9–1.0             | 50,000 | 62.3%             | 56.9%        |

**Observation:** Accuracy is relatively flat across the context (~57–59%), with a modest peak at bins 6–7 (60–80% of context used). The drop at bin 9 is notable: despite having the longest context (and hence the highest majority baseline due to class imbalance), the probe does *not* improve — suggesting that very late tokens in long contexts may be less linearly decodable, or that long trajectories have noisier outcome signals.

### Axis 2: Tool-Call Index

| Bin | Episode position | n    | Majority baseline | Val accuracy |
|-----|-----------------|------|-------------------|--------------|
| 0   | earliest 10%    | 947  | 52.8%             | **58.2%**    |
| 1   |                 | 811  | 52.4%             | 61.7%        |
| 2   |                 | 826  | 52.4%             | 60.0%        |
| 3   |                 | 820  | 52.7%             | 61.6%        |
| 4   |                 | 800  | 53.3%             | 62.5%        |
| 5   |                 | 872  | 53.4%             | 64.9%        |
| 6   |                 | 846  | 53.1%             | 61.5%        |
| 7   |                 | 822  | 54.0%             | 62.2%        |
| 8   |                 | 848  | 53.2%             | 61.5%        |
| 9   | latest 10%      | 975  | 52.2%             | **67.7%**    |

**Observation:** Clear upward trend — the model's hidden state becomes increasingly informative about the final outcome as the episode progresses. The last decile of tool calls (bin 9) is substantially more predictive (67.7%) than the first (58.2%). This is consistent with the model progressively accumulating task-completion signal.

### Axis 3: Stage

| Stage       | n     | Majority baseline | Val accuracy |
|-------------|-------|-------------------|--------------|
| exploration | 3,652 | 51.8%             | **57.3%**    |
| other-bash  | 2,202 | 57.5%             | 58.6%        |
| testing     | 1,376 | 53.0%             | 62.9%        |
| editing     | 1,085 | 57.0%             | 65.9%        |
| submission  | 252   | 56.0%             | **68.0%**    |

**Observation:** Stage is the most discriminating axis. Submission activations are most predictive of outcome (68.0%), followed closely by editing (65.9%). This makes intuitive sense: when the model writes a patch (editing) or commits to a final answer (submission), the hidden state must encode whether the solution is correct. Exploration activations are least predictive — early browsing of the repo does not yet carry strong outcome signal.

---

## Key Takeaways

1. **Outcome is linearly decodable from layer-32 activations at above-chance accuracy across all conditions** (~57–68% vs ~52% majority baseline).

2. **The strongest signal is in late-episode, task-committing actions.** Both the tool-call index axis (bin 9: 67.7%) and the stage axis (submission: 68.0%, editing: 65.9%) point to the same conclusion: the model "knows" whether it is going to succeed most clearly at the moment it acts on that knowledge.

3. **Token position within the context window matters less than episode position.** The relatively flat token-position curve (57–59%) contrasts with the steeper tool-call index trend (58–68%), suggesting that *what type of action a token belongs to* is more informative than *where in the raw context it sits*.

4. **Exploration is least predictive.** The model gathers information early without yet committing to an outcome representation — outcome decodability is low (57.3%) when the agent is browsing files and reading code.

## Limitations & Next Steps

- **~50% file yield** due to TP-rank filtering — only even-rank files have real activations. A future extraction could aggregate across TP ranks to double the usable data.
- **Single layer (32).** Probing across all 64 layers would reveal at which depth outcome information first emerges and where it peaks.
- **Linear probe only.** A nonlinear probe (e.g. small MLP) might reveal stronger signal, though linear probes are preferred for interpretability.
- **Subsampled activations** (5,000 per file cap) — full-data training might improve accuracy, especially for the token-position axis where n=50k was the cap per bin.
- **Steering vectors.** Having established that layer-32 activations carry outcome information, the natural next step is to compute mean-difference steering vectors (pass − fail) and intervene during generation to see if outcome can be causally influenced.
